record.title: Public-sector wage cap (Bill 124) ruled unconstitutional, then repealed
record.summary: Bill 124 capped compensation increases for broader public-sector workers at 1% a year for three years. The Superior Court found it violated the Charter’s freedom of association and declared it void. The Court of Appeal upheld that ruling for unionized employees. The government did not appeal further and repealed the act. News reports cited a Financial Accountability Office estimate of about $13.7 billion in retroactive compensation.
record.government_position: On February 12, 2024 the government said it would not appeal and would repeal Bill 124 in its entirety, with regulations in the meantime to exempt non-unionized workers.
timeline: Superior Court declares the act void (2022 ONSC 6658)
Court of Appeal upholds the ruling for unionized employees (2024 ONCA 101); government says it will not appeal
Act repealed in full by Order in Council

record.summary: Bill 254 doubled the pre-election period in which third-party political advertising spending is limited, from 6 to 12 months. After the Superior Court found that change unconstitutional, the government re-enacted it in Bill 307 using the notwithstanding clause, making it the first Ontario law to use the clause. (Bill 31 had invoked it in 2018 but never passed.) The Court of Appeal found the clause was validly used but that the limits breached the right to vote, which the clause cannot override. The Supreme Court of Canada upheld that ruling 5–4.
record.government_position: In 2021 the government said the notwithstanding clause was needed to preserve the limits. In 2023 the Attorney General’s office said it was disappointed and would appeal. After the 2025 ruling, the province said it would review the decision.
timeline: Superior Court strikes down the 12-month period (2021 ONSC 4076)
Bill 307 passes and receives royal assent, invoking the notwithstanding clause, four days after first reading
Court of Appeal finds the limits breach the right to vote (2023 ONCA 139)
Supreme Court of Canada dismisses Ontario’s appeal, 5–4 (2025 SCC 5)

record.title: Toronto council cut to 25 wards (Bill 5): government won at the Supreme Court
record.summary: Bill 5 cut Toronto’s council from 47 to 25 wards during the 2018 municipal campaign. The Superior Court found it unconstitutional, and the government introduced Bill 31 to re-enact it with the notwithstanding clause. The Court of Appeal stayed the ruling, the election went ahead with 25 wards, and Bill 31 was never voted on. The Court of Appeal and then the Supreme Court of Canada (5–4) ruled for the province.
record.government_position: After the stay, the province said it would not bring Bill 31 to a vote while the stay was in effect. It said it was pleased with the 2019 Court of Appeal ruling.
timeline: Superior Court finds a Charter breach (2018 ONSC 5151)
Bill 31 introduced with the notwithstanding clause
Court of Appeal stays the ruling
Court of Appeal rules 3–2 for Ontario
Supreme Court of Canada dismisses Toronto’s appeal, 5–4 (2021 SCC 34)

record.title: Toronto bike lane removal (Bill 212): struck down, then upheld on appeal
record.summary: Bill 212 required the removal of bike lanes on Bloor Street, Yonge Street and University Avenue in Toronto. The Superior Court found the requirement breached the Charter’s right to life, liberty and security of the person. The Court of Appeal unanimously overturned that ruling. Cycle Toronto has said it will seek leave to appeal to the Supreme Court; whether leave has been granted could not be confirmed.
record.government_position: The government appealed the 2025 ruling. After the 2026 decision, the transportation minister said bike lanes belong on secondary roads, not in vehicle lanes on the busiest streets.
timeline: Superior Court finds a Charter breach (2025 ONSC 4397)
Court of Appeal overturns the ruling (2026 ONCA 582)

record.title: Greenbelt land removed, then restored (Bill 136)
record.summary: In December 2022 the province removed about 7,400 acres from 15 Greenbelt areas and added about 9,400 acres elsewhere. The Auditor General found the site selection was biased and favoured certain developers, and that the landowners could see more than $8.3 billion in increased property value. The Integrity Commissioner found the housing minister contravened the Members’ Integrity Act. The Premier reversed the decision, and Bill 136 restored the lands. The RCMP opened an investigation in October 2023; its last public update, in October 2025, said it was ongoing with no charges.
record.government_position: The original rationale was to enable at least 50,000 homes with a net Greenbelt expansion. Announcing the reversal, the Premier said: “It was a mistake to open the Greenbelt.”
timeline: Integrity Commissioner’s report on the housing minister
Bill 136 receives royal assent, restoring the lands

record.title: Provincial changes to 12 municipal official plans reversed (Bill 150)
record.summary: In 2022 and 2023 the province changed the official plans of 12 municipalities, including Barrie, Hamilton, Ottawa, Peel and York, many of them to expand urban boundaries. In October 2023 the government announced it would reverse those changes. Bill 150 deemed the decisions never made and limited claims for compensation.
record.government_position: The housing minister said the decisions failed to support housing goals and earn public confidence, that the former minister’s office had been too involved, and that the province would cover municipalities’ costs for work already done.

record.title: Peel Region dissolution passed, then cancelled (Bills 112 and 185)
record.summary: Bill 112 would have dissolved the Region of Peel on January 1, 2025, making Mississauga, Brampton and Caledon single-tier cities. Six months after it became law, the government announced it would not proceed. Bill 185 repealed the dissolution.
record.government_position: The housing minister said municipal leaders had warned that full dissolution would lead to significant tax increases and disruption to services.
timeline: Government announces it will not dissolve Peel
Bill 185 royal assent, repealing the dissolution

record.title: Education workers’ back-to-work law (Bill 28) repealed 11 days after passing
record.summary: Bill 28 imposed contracts on CUPE school-board education workers and banned strikes, and used the notwithstanding clause pre-emptively. It passed three days after it was introduced. After CUPE agreed to end its walkout, the government repealed it with Bill 35, which passed in a single day and deemed Bill 28 never to have been in force.
record.government_position: The Premier said the government was willing to rescind the law “as a gesture of good faith” if CUPE ended its walkout. The education minister said the government would revoke Bill 28 in its entirety and return to the bargaining table.
timeline: Bill 28 passes and receives royal assent
Government commits to repeal; CUPE ends walkout
Bill 35 passes all readings and receives royal assent

record.title: Paid sick days: three NDP bills defeated; government passed a temporary program
record.summary: The NDP’s Stay Home If You Are Sick Act was defeated at second reading three times. The first version proposed 7 paid personal emergency leave days plus 14 paid days during an infectious disease emergency; the later versions proposed 10 paid days and 14 during an emergency. Eight weeks after the first defeat, the government passed Bill 284, which provided up to 3 paid days of COVID-19 leave at up to $200 a day, reimbursed through the WSIB. That program ended on March 31, 2023.
record.government_position: When the program ended, the province said it had served its purpose and pointed to Ontario’s high vaccination rate.
timeline: Government Bill 284 passes in one day: up to 3 paid days

record.title: Four hours of daily care in long-term care: NDP bills stalled; government set a target
record.summary: The NDP’s Time to Care Act would have required an average of at least 4 hours of direct care per long-term care resident per day. It passed second reading twice with no votes against (80–0 and 73–0) and stalled in committee both times. The government’s Bill 37 set a provincewide average target of 4 hours by March 31, 2025. The ministry reported 3 hours 49 minutes (95.5% of the target) at that deadline; the government later said the target was surpassed in spring 2025.
record.government_position: The ministry cited recruitment and retention challenges, especially in rural and remote communities. A later government release said the province averaged 4 hours 5 minutes in the first quarter of 2025–26.
timeline: NDP Bill 13 passes second reading 80–0; referred to committee
NDP Bill 14 passes second reading 73–0; referred to committee
Government Bill 37 royal assent, setting the 4-hour target

integrity.title: Integrity Commissioner report on Premier Ford and the appointment of the OPP Commissioner
who: Doug Ford (Premier)
integrity.subject: Conflict of interest
integrity.summary: On requests from opposition MPPs, the Commissioner inquired into whether Premier Ford breached the Members' Integrity Act in the appointment of his friend Ron Taverner as OPP Commissioner. He found no breach of the sections alleged but found the recruitment process flawed.
findings: “Premier Ford did not breach any of the sections of the Act, as alleged.”
“The Premier stayed at arm’s length from the recruitment process and … believed it to be independent.”
The Commissioner found “some troubling aspects of the recruitment process” and concluded the process was flawed.
Recommended an independent, transparent appointment process for the OPP Commissioner.
integrity.consequence: No breach found; no penalty. Process recommendation only.

integrity.title: Integrity Commissioner report on Minister Bethlenfalvy and a social media ad strategy
who: Peter Bethlenfalvy (President of the Treasury Board)
integrity.subject: Other
integrity.summary: On a request from MPP Taras Natyshak, the Commissioner examined whether the Minister breached the Act or parliamentary convention through his staff’s social media ad-spend strategy. He found government resources were used for a partisan purpose but did not attribute the breach to the Minister.
findings: “Minister Bethlenfalvy did not breach the MIA or parliamentary convention.”
Government resources, including staff salaried time, “were used for a partisan purpose” in a strategy targeting likely PC supporters, to be funded by the MPP’s riding association.
The Minister “did not appreciate the significance of the ad spend strategy” and “never approved” it.
Made five recommendations on staff training, approval processes and social media guidelines.
integrity.consequence: No breach by the Minister; recommendations only.

integrity.title: Integrity Commissioner report on Stan Cho and partisan meetings held from a ministry office
who: Stan Cho (MPP; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance)
integrity.subject: Other
integrity.summary: On a request from MPP Stephen Blais, the Commissioner found Mr. Cho breached parliamentary convention by using his Ministry of Finance office to take part in partisan meetings.
findings: “Mr. Cho breached parliamentary convention by using his Ministry of Finance office to participate remotely in partisan meetings.”
He “failed to provide adequate supervision, direction and training to his staff”.
Recommended training of MPP staff on the ethics rules and conventions.
integrity.consequence: Breach of parliamentary convention found; no penalty recommended.

integrity.title: Integrity Commissioner report on Catherine Fife (NDP) and a budget-feedback email
who: Catherine Fife (MPP, Official Opposition)
integrity.subject: Other
integrity.summary: On a request from PC MPP Dave Smith, the Commissioner found an opposition MPP breached parliamentary convention when an email from her legislative account linked to a partisan webpage. Included so the record covers all parties.
findings: “It is my opinion that Ms. Fife breached Ontario parliamentary convention with respect to the sending of this email.”
The Commissioner found it “was never her intent” to link to the partisan site, but she did not exercise due diligence.
Recommended no penalty because the breach was inadvertent and promptly addressed.
integrity.consequence: Breach found; no penalty recommended.

integrity.title: Integrity Commissioner report on Vijay Thanigasalam and a virtual town hall
who: Vijay Thanigasalam (MPP, Scarborough—Rouge Park)
integrity.subject: Other
integrity.summary: On a request from MPP Taras Natyshak, the Commissioner found the MPP breached parliamentary convention in the organization of an April 9, 2021 virtual town hall that acknowledged the PC candidate for a neighbouring riding.
findings: “It is my opinion that Mr. Thanigasalam breached Ontario parliamentary convention with respect to the organization and conduct of this town hall.”
“It was not his intent to hold a partisan event”; his staff introduced partisan aspects.
He is responsible for his staff’s errors “because he did not adequately train or supervise them”.
integrity.consequence: Breach found; no penalty recommended because staff training was arranged.

integrity.title: Integrity Commissioner report on Stephen Crawford and long-term care investments
who: Stephen Crawford (MPP; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Infrastructure)
integrity.subject: Conflict of interest
integrity.summary: On a request from MPP Stephen Blais, the Commissioner examined whether holding investments in long-term care companies created a conflict when Mr. Crawford took part in the Long-Term Care Development Program and Bill 218. He found no breach.
findings: Mr. Crawford had no influence in the decision-making process on the Long-Term Care Development Program.
Bill 218 was “a law of general application”, so a private interest was not engaged; no breach of sections 2 or 4.
Recommended the Legislature consider extending investment restrictions to members and parliamentary assistants.
integrity.consequence: No breach found.

integrity.title: Integrity Commissioner report on Jessica Bell (NDP) and partisan symbols on constituency materials
who: Jessica Bell (MPP, Official Opposition)
integrity.subject: Other
integrity.summary: On a request from PC MPP Mike Harris, the Commissioner found an opposition MPP breached parliamentary convention by including NDP logos and riding association references in constituency event materials. Included so the record covers all parties.
findings: “Ms. Bell contravened the Ontario parliamentary convention against using constituency resources for partisan purposes.”
She “promptly admitted her error” and cooperated fully.
Recommended no penalty.
integrity.consequence: Breach found; no penalty recommended.

integrity.title: Integrity Commissioner report on Randy Hillier (No. 1): constituency resources used for partisan purposes
who: Randy Hillier (MPP, Lanark—Frontenac—Kingston)
integrity.subject: Other
integrity.summary: On a request from MPP Ian Arthur, the Commissioner found Mr. Hillier breached parliamentary convention in three ways involving constituency office resources and constituent contact information used for partisan messages. He dismissed the allegation of a private-interest conflict.
findings: Breached “the parliamentary convention against using constituency office resources for partisan purposes in three different ways”, including letting his daughter film her federal candidacy announcement in his constituency office.
Directed staff to perform partisan activities without an accountability framework.
Collected constituent contact information into two databases and used it to send partisan messages.
integrity.consequence: Reprimand recommended to the Legislative Assembly.

integrity.title: Integrity Commissioner report on Randy Hillier (No. 2): social media posts naming individuals
who: Randy Hillier (MPP, Lanark—Frontenac—Kingston)
integrity.subject: Other
integrity.summary: On a request from MPP Peggy Sattler, the Commissioner found social media posts naming and showing individuals who had become seriously ill or died, with an unfounded claim that COVID-19 vaccines were involved, breached parliamentary convention.
findings: The posts “amounted to a breach of parliamentary convention that might readily be presumed”.
The Commissioner weighed the Assembly’s swift censure, Mr. Hillier’s public apology and his admission of mistakes.
integrity.consequence: Reprimand recommended to the Legislative Assembly.

integrity.title: Integrity Commissioner report on Minister Clark and the 2022 Greenbelt removals
who: Steve Clark (Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing)
Ryan Amato (Chief of Staff to Minister Clark)
integrity.subject: Greenbelt
integrity.summary: On a request from MPP Marit Stiles, the Commissioner inquired into the decision to remove or redesignate lands in the Greenbelt. He concluded Minister Clark breached sections 2 and 3(2) of the Members’ Integrity Act, largely through his chief of staff’s conduct, which he attributed to the Minister.
findings: “Minister Clark breached sections 2 and 3(2) of the Act.”
Mr. Amato “was the driving force behind a flawed process which provided an advantage to those who approached him.”
Of 15 properties removed or redesignated, Mr. Amato “was involved in the selection of 14”.
Mr. Amato’s communications to developers “must be attributed to Mr. Clark” because he failed to oversee an important initiative in his ministry.
The Commissioner believed the Minister was unaware of that process.
integrity.consequence: Reprimand recommended to the Legislative Assembly. Mr. Clark apologized. Whether the Assembly adopted the reprimand was not confirmed.

response.text: “I regret that I didn’t provide the sufficient oversight,” and “the buck stops with me.” Mr. Clark did not resign.

integrity.title: Auditor General special report on changes to the Greenbelt
who: Ministry of Municipal Affairs and Housing
Ryan Amato (Chief of Staff to the Housing Minister)
integrity.subject: Greenbelt
integrity.summary: The Auditor General examined the 2022 removal of 15 sites from the Greenbelt. She concluded site selection was not transparent, fair, objective or fully informed.
findings: “How the land sites were selected was not transparent, fair, objective, or fully informed.”
There was sufficient land for the 1.5 million homes target “without the need to build on the Greenbelt”.
“Direct access to the Housing Minister’s Chief of Staff resulted in certain prominent developers receiving preferential treatment.”
About 92% of the roughly 7,400 acres removed came from five sites put forward by two developers.
Owners could see more than $8.3 billion in added land value.
integrity.consequence: The government restored the lands (Bill 136, December 2023). A 2025 follow-up found 95% of the Auditor General’s recommended actions fully implemented.
timeline: Bill 136 royal assent, restoring the lands

integrity.title: Integrity Commissioner: no inquiry into Premier Ford and two family wedding events
who: Doug Ford (Premier)
integrity.subject: Fundraising
integrity.summary: On a February 2023 request from MPP Marit Stiles about a stag and doe and a wedding for the Premier’s daughter, the Commissioner found insufficient grounds to hold an inquiry into breaches of sections 2, 4 or 6(1).
findings: “There are insufficient grounds … to warrant an inquiry as to whether Premier Ford breached sections 2, 4 or sub-section 6(1) of the Act.”
The Act “does not concern itself with appearances of a conflict, only actual conflicts” (interim report).
Only one developer with Greenbelt removals attended the wedding.
integrity.consequence: No inquiry; no finding of breach.

integrity.title: RCMP criminal investigation related to the Greenbelt
who: Government of Ontario figures (not publicly named by the RCMP)
integrity.subject: Greenbelt
integrity.summary: The RCMP opened a criminal investigation after the Auditor General and Integrity Commissioner reports. The last public update, in October 2025, said it was ongoing; reports in October 2026 say there are no updates.
findings: The RCMP has said the investigation is ongoing and has withheld details to protect it.
No charges have been announced.
integrity.consequence: No charges or conclusion reported as of November 2026.

integrity.title: Integrity Commissioner closes an inquiry into Kaleed Rasheed without a finding
who: Kaleed Rasheed (former Minister of Public and Business Service Delivery)
integrity.subject: Greenbelt
integrity.summary: An inquiry requested by MPP Marit Stiles in October 2023 concerned a 2020 Las Vegas trip with a Greenbelt-linked developer. The office closed it without a finding because inquiries must be suspended when an election is called and the requester did not ask to restart it.
findings: Under the Act, an inquiry is suspended when an election is called and resumes only if the requester asks within 30 days afterwards. That did not happen.
No finding on Mr. Rasheed was made.
integrity.consequence: Inquiry closed with no finding. Mr. Rasheed left cabinet in November 2023.

response.text: Mr. Rasheed called a mistake in dates he gave the Commissioner “an honest mistake”.

timeline: Commissioner says he will not investigate the trip “at this time” (CTV)

integrity.title: Auditor General audit of the Ontario Place redevelopment
who: Ministry of Infrastructure
Infrastructure Ontario
integrity.subject: Procurement
integrity.summary: The Auditor General audited the call for development for Ontario Place. She found the process was not fair, transparent or accountable to all participants and that many rules were not followed.
findings: The process was “not fair, transparent, or accountable to all participants”; criteria were finalized after the deadline.
Three bidders met with the ministry and the Premier’s Office during the open period, “contrary to CFD Rules”.
An Infrastructure Ontario vice-president communicated directly with Therme during the communications ban; no minutes of bidder meetings were kept.
Estimated public cost rose by $1.8 billion since 2019, to $2.2 billion.
integrity.consequence: The Public Accounts Committee held hearings in November 2025 and reported in October 2026. No minister was found in breach.

response.text: Deputy Premier Sylvia Jones, answering for the minister, said she saw no reason the minister should step down (paraphrased by Global News).

integrity.title: Auditor General finding that the zoning order process needs an overhaul
who: Ministry of Municipal Affairs and Housing
integrity.subject: MZOs
integrity.summary: The Auditor General’s 2024 annual report found the minister’s zoning order process needed to be overhauled. According to the Canadian Press, Ontario used zoning orders 114 times from 2019 to 2023, 17 times as often as in the previous two decades.
findings: “No protocol or rationale for prioritizing some zoning order requests over others.”
The ministry did not give the minister complete and timely information about incoming requests.
Recommended recording the reasoning for each order.

integrity.title: Integrity Commissioner: no inquiry into Minister Surma and the Ontario Place project
who: Kinga Surma (Minister of Infrastructure)
integrity.subject: Procurement
integrity.summary: On an October 2024 request from MPP Marit Stiles, the Commissioner found insufficient grounds to inquire into whether Minister Surma breached sections 2 and 3 over Ontario Place and the Therme agreement. He did not examine whether the process itself was flawed.
findings: “There are insufficient grounds for me to conduct an inquiry into whether Minister Surma breached either section 2 or section 3 of the Act.”
The Act does not cover “apparent” conflicts of interest.
The Minister’s counsel disputed the alleged irregularities.
integrity.consequence: No inquiry; no finding.

integrity.title: Lobbyist Registrar publishes non-compliance by consultant lobbyist Nico Fidani-Diker
who: Nico Fidani-Diker (consultant lobbyist)
integrity.subject: Lobbying
integrity.summary: The Registrar found a consultant lobbyist did not comply with the Lobbyists Registration Act on several matters, including Greenbelt removals and zoning-order filings, and published his name rather than imposing a ban.
findings: Failed to register after lobbying a public office holder on a client’s Greenbelt removal request in 2022.
Offered two public office holders hockey tickets, placing them “in a position of real or potential conflict of interest”.
Contravened the conflict prohibition in lobbying two public office holders with whom he had close working, political and personal relationships.
Failed to give particulars of the regulation change sought in two filings (a Greenbelt regulation and a zoning order).
integrity.consequence: Name and summary published; no lobbying ban.

response.text: “These oversights were mine and mine alone.” He accepted “full responsibility”.

integrity.title: Lobbyist Registrar bans John Mutton from lobbying for two years
who: John Mutton (consultant lobbyist; former mayor of Clarington)
integrity.subject: Lobbying
integrity.summary: The Registrar found repeated non-compliance with the Lobbyists Registration Act between 2016 and 2023, including unregistered lobbying on zoning orders and the Greenbelt, contingency fees, gifts and a political fundraiser. The Registrar’s public summary does not name the public office holders involved.
findings: Failed to register after lobbying two public office holders on a client’s zoning-order request; paid a $300,000 contingency fee.
Lobbied on a Greenbelt removal; offered a round of golf and Raptors tickets; paid a $225,000 contingency fee.
Lobbied on a second client’s zoning order for a $100,000 contingency fee, and in 2023 on a third client’s for a $250,000 contingency fee not yet payable.
“Organized a political fundraiser raising more than $25,000 for the public office holder’s riding association approximately two months prior to the beginning of the 2022 provincial election.”
Conduct “undermine[s] the Act’s purpose of transparency and public confidence in the independence of public sector decision making.”
integrity.consequence: Prohibited from lobbying Ontario public office holders from April 17, 2025 to April 17, 2027; name and summary published.

integrity.title: Registrar’s report on lobbyist John Mutton is reported to quote texts with PC MPP Laurie Scott about zoning orders and fundraising
who: Laurie Scott (PC MPP, Haliburton—Kawartha Lakes—Brock)
John Mutton (consultant lobbyist)
integrity.subject: MZOs
integrity.summary: A 132-page Lobbyist Registrar report on Mr. Mutton, dated January 29, 2025 and supplied to The Trillium by Mr. Mutton, quotes text messages between Ms. Scott and Mr. Mutton from December 2021 to July 2023. The report concerns Mr. Mutton’s compliance with the Lobbyists Registration Act. It made no formal ruling on Ms. Scott’s conduct. This entry relies on The Highlander’s reporting because The Trillium’s article could not be opened.
findings: As reported by The Highlander: the Commissioner found Mr. Mutton breached the Act about a dozen times and put Ms. Scott “in a position of potential conflict of interest”.

The report found Ms. Scott and Mr. Mutton “clearly communicated in an effort to move forward” a provincial zoning-order decision. The orders concerned Kawartha Downs and Brown’s Line in Cavan Monaghan.
The Commissioner did not determine whether Ms. Scott meaningfully helped either order be approved, and made no formal ruling on her conduct.
A text of February 2, 2023, as quoted: “do you think you could get a couple of your people … They have to go thru my portal so I get credit.”
integrity.consequence: No finding against Ms. Scott. As of November 6, 2026 no inquiry into her has been confirmed open. The Highlander reports NDP Leader Marit Stiles asked the Integrity Commissioner to investigate.

response.text: Her office received a zoning-order request endorsed by the municipality, and the order followed the ministry’s established process. “All information on donations and donors is publicly available.” (as reported; full statement not seen)
response.by: Laurie Scott, statement to The Trillium and The Highlander

ledger.said: Bill 245 would cut the time Ontarians spend waiting for their day in court.
ledger.measure: Criminal cases stayed for unreasonable delay under the Jordan time limits.
evidence: 191 provincially prosecuted cases stayed for delay since July 2016 (Auditor General, 2019 audit).
More than 580 stayed from 2016 through 2023, with 59 sexual assault cases stayed in 2023, the most in any year (ministry data via CBC).
Charges for crimes against a person rose from about 57,000 in 2015 to about 80,000 in 2025, and withdrawn charges are rising (CP24).
ledger.side: His office says stays for delay are under 0.1% of cases, and points to up to 52 new judges and nearly 700 more Crowns, victim support and court staff.
ledger.context: Much of the backlog predates him, and the pandemic and growth in digital evidence added to it.

ledger.said: The Landlord and Tenant Board’s own standard is a hearing within 30 days. The board sits under his ministry through Tribunals Ontario.
evidence: The Ombudsman found the board fundamentally failing, with waits of seven to eight months and up to two years, and made 61 recommendations.
Backlog down from 53,057 to 41,465 cases, with processing times of three to seven months. Adjudicators up from 51 in 2018–19 to 133 (Tribunal Watch, from the annual report).
ledger.side: The ministry says it funded more adjudicators and a new case management system, and the backlog has fallen from its peak.
ledger.context: Improving, but still far from the 30-day standard and from pre-2019 levels.

ledger.said: Merge five land tribunals into one Ontario Land Tribunal and widen judicial appointment shortlists from two names to six.
evidence: Bill 245 received royal assent on April 19, 2021.
ledger.context: Delivered as promised. Whether it sped up appointments is a separate, disputed question.

ledger.said: No further cuts to the legal aid budget after the 2019 cut of $133 million.
evidence: Legal Aid Ontario raised income eligibility for duty counsel and criminal certificates to $45,440 for families of up to four, which it says reaches about 180,000 more people a year.
His press secretary said the agency’s strong financial position made the increase possible, which critics read as no new provincial money (a defence lawyer’s column).
ledger.side: Legal Aid Ontario framed the expansion as supporting the province’s goal of reducing the criminal court backlog.
ledger.context: No sign of further cuts after 2019, and no sign of the 2019 cut being restored either. Provincial funding figures from Legal Aid Ontario’s annual reports would settle it.

ledger.said: Connect every resident to a family doctor or nurse practitioner by 2029, which he called fairly ambitious, but achievable.
ledger.measure: Unattached patients in the riding, against the 2029 deadline.
evidence: $6.6 million for the Barrie Community Health Centre and Barrie and Community Family Health Team, expected to connect nearly 20,000 unattached residents, with new sites in north Barrie and Angus.
ledger.context: Track attachment numbers each year until 2029.

ledger.said: $18.5 million for the Mapleview Drive East and Yonge Street expansion, to unlock 11,900 new homes.
ledger.measure: Road work finished, then homes built in the area.
ledger.context: Too early to judge. The homes figure is a projection, not a count.

bills.title: Smarter and Stronger Justice Act
bills.what: Amended more than 20 acts: rewrote the Legal Aid Services Act, changed class action rules, allowed online verification of identity and legal documents, and simplified small estates.
bills.critics: Critics said the legal aid rewrite dropped access to justice from the system’s stated purpose.

bills.title: Accelerating Access to Justice Act
bills.what: Created the Ontario Land Tribunal, widened judicial shortlists from two to six and let the Attorney General reject a list, made virtual witnessing of wills permanent, and expanded French-language filing.
bills.critics: Critics said the appointment changes gave the Attorney General too much say over who becomes a judge.

bills.title: Ends fixed election dates, raises the donation limit to $5,000
bills.what: Downey announced these reforms in October 2025. They passed inside the Finance Minister’s fall budget bill, Bill 68, under a time-allocation motion that limited debate. Fixed election dates are gone, though a five-year maximum between elections still applies. The donation limit rises from $3,400 to $5,000, and the per-vote subsidy to parties becomes permanent.
bills.critics: Opposition parties said it favours big donors and the governing party, and that ending fixed dates lets the government pick the timing.

bills.title: Protecting Ontario Elections Act, then the Protecting Elections and Defending Democracy Act
bills.what: Bill 254 doubled donation limits and tightened limits on third-party political advertising in the year before an election. In June 2021 the Ontario Superior Court found the advertising limits violated freedom of expression. The government recalled the legislature and re-passed them as Bill 307 using the notwithstanding clause, a first in Ontario. Downey supported the move as protecting elections from outside influence. The Court of Appeal struck Bill 307 down in 2023, and the Supreme Court of Canada upheld that ruling.
bills.critics: Unions and civil liberties groups said the limits were designed to silence critics of the government before an election.

bills.title: Enhancing Access to Justice Act
bills.what: A justice-system omnibus he moved to third reading in March 2024, pitched as improving access to justice, community safety and court modernization.
